If you do want to grow it from seed, chill the seed in the refrigerator for a few weeks first, then surface-sow it and do not cover it, since it needs light to sprout; keep it around 70°F, start indoors about 10 weeks before your last frost, and be patient, because it comes up slowly and unevenly.

seasoned: Plant lavender lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine other plants want, set it in the sunniest, sharpest-draining spot, and on clay build a mound or raised bed rather than digging in sand. Rich, wet soil is what kills lavender.

beginner: Leave about 18 to 24 inches between plants. That space lets air move around each one, which helps prevent the fungal problems lavender can get when it stays damp.
seasoned: Space plants 18 to 24 inches apart and give each one room to breathe. Good air circulation between plants is one of the simplest ways to head off the fungal problems lavender is prone to in damp conditions.

beginner: The first year is about growing roots, not flowers. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water deeply but less often. Pinch off the first few flowers and lightly shape it so it grows bushy. It takes about three years to reach full size.
seasoned: Year one is about roots, not flowers. Water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper toward deep and infrequent. Pinch the first flowers and lightly shape the plant so it builds out bushy; it will reach full size in about three years and live well over a decade.

beginner: Try not to feed it. Lavender needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives you lots of leaves but fewer flowers. The same is true for water, where more is not better.
seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Lavender has low fertility needs, and over-fertilizing produces soft leafy growth at the expense of flowers. The same goes for water: more is not better.

beginner: In spring, look for new green growth low on the plant. That means it survived winter. As the weather warms, water deeply but not very often instead of a little bit every day.
seasoned: Watch for fresh green growth low on the plant each spring; that is your signal it came through winter. As the soil warms, settle into deep but infrequent watering rather than frequent shallow sips.

beginner: If you waited until spring to do the big trim, do it once you see green growth and frost is over. Cut only into the green parts, because the hard woody stems below will not grow back.
seasoned: If you saved a hard prune for spring, make it once green growth has emerged and frost has passed, around early in the season. Cut into green growth only; the bare woody stems below will not resprout.

beginner: For the best scent and color, cut the flower stems when the bottom flowers on each spike are just starting to open, not when fully bloomed. Cut in the morning after the dew dries.
seasoned: For the best fragrance and dried color, cut flower stems as the lowest flowers on each spike begin to open, rather than waiting for full bloom. Harvest in the morning once the dew has dried.

beginner: To dry it, tie small bunches and hang them upside down somewhere warm and airy, then store the dried flowers in a sealed jar. If you want to cook with it, use only your own lavender that has not been sprayed, and the English kind works best.
seasoned: To dry lavender, gather small bundles and hang them upside down somewhere warm, dark, and airy, then store the dried flowers sealed. For cooking, use only your own unsprayed lavender, never florist or nursery stock, and English types most of all.

beginner: This trim is what keeps lavender going. After it finishes flowering, cut about a third off the plant, going only into the soft green growth and never down into the hard woody stems, because those will not grow back. Skip it year after year and the plant gets tall and woody, flops open in the middle, and slowly dies.
seasoned: This is the cut that keeps lavender alive. After bloom fades, shear the whole plant back by about a third, cutting into soft green growth only and never into the bare woody base, which will not resprout. Skip this yearly cut and the plant turns leggy, splits open at the center, and declines within a few years.

beginner: Do the big trim after it flowers, not in the middle of summer. Trimming in July cuts off flowers that are still forming, so wait until the main bloom has faded.
seasoned: Time the cut after flowering, not in midsummer. A July prune removes the season's blooms while they are still developing, so wait until the main flush has faded before you shear.

beginner: In winter, do almost nothing. Stop watering and feeding, and save the big trim for spring. A resting plant sitting in wet soil rots, and a late trim leaves it weak, so do not water it or cut it back now.
seasoned: Over winter, do almost nothing: stop watering and feeding, and leave any hard pruning for spring. A dormant plant in wet soil rots, and a fresh fall cut leaves it vulnerable, so the worst things you can do are water it and prune it late.

beginner: Shelter the tender kinds. Spanish and French lavender are not cold hardy, so grow them in pots you can bring somewhere protected for winter. English lavender can stay outside through cold winters if it has good drainage and a sheltered spot.
seasoned: Protect the tender types. Spanish and French lavenders are not cold hardy and are best grown in containers brought under cover for winter, while English lavender overwinters outdoors through about zone 5, or zone 4 with good drainage and a sheltered, mulched spot.

beginner: A grown lavender gives you plenty of flower stems each summer, enough to cut for the house and to dry, especially once it is a few years old.
seasoned: A mature plant yields many cuttable flower spikes each summer (often dozens of stems), enough for fresh bouquets plus bundles for drying; productivity peaks once the plant reaches full size at about three years.

beginner: Do not expect much the first year. Trimming off the first flowers helps the plant bulk up for bigger harvests later.
seasoned: Expect little to no usable harvest the first year; pinching early flowers to build a bushy framework pays off in later seasons.

beginner: Leaves turning yellow or the plant dying back
seasoned: Yellowing leaves or dieback

beginner: For lavender, yellow leaves and dieback usually mean too much water, not too little. Overwatering and soggy soil are the biggest killer. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
seasoned: With lavender, yellowing and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering and poor drainage are the number one killer, leading to root and crown rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.

beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but only once in a while, and on heavy soil plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.
seasoned: Cut back on watering hard and fix drainage. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and on clay use a mound or raised bed. Never let lavender sit in wet ground.

beginner: Tall and woody with a gap in the middle
seasoned: Leggy, woody, split-open center

beginner: When lavender gets tall and woody and splits open in the middle, it missed its yearly trim. Without that trim after flowering, it stops staying bushy and slowly falls apart.
seasoned: A plant that has gone leggy and woody and flopped open at the center missed its annual cut-back. Without the yearly post-bloom prune, lavender stops renewing its compact form and declines within a few years.

beginner: Trim about a third off every year after it flowers, cutting only into the green and never into the hard wood, which will not grow back. A plant that is already very woody often cannot be saved and may be worth replacing.
seasoned: Shear by about a third every year after bloom, cutting into green growth only and never into the bare wood, which will not resprout. A badly overgrown plant often cannot be fully renovated and may be better replaced.

beginner: Hardly any flowers
seasoned: Few or no flowers

beginner: Few flowers usually means too much fertilizer or too much shade. Feeding it too much gives leaves instead of flowers, and lavender needs full sun to bloom.
seasoned: Sparse flowering usually means too much feed or too much shade. Over-fertilizing drives soft leafy growth at the expense of blooms, and lavender needs full sun to flower well.

beginner: Stop feeding it and make sure it gets full sun. Lavender needs very little, and poor, dry, sunny conditions give you the most flowers.
seasoned: Stop fertilizing and make sure the plant gets full sun. Lavender has low fertility needs, and lean, dry, sunny conditions produce the most flowers.

beginner: Lavender and your pets
seasoned: Pets and lavender

beginner: Lavender is fine for people in small amounts in cooking, but eating a lot is mildly toxic, and it can make cats, dogs, and horses sick. Good to know, not a reason to skip it.
seasoned: Lavender is edible in small culinary amounts for people but is a low-severity toxin in quantity, and it is a hazard to cats, dogs, and horses, which can react to its compounds (linalool and linalyl acetate). This is worth knowing, not a reason to avoid growing it.

beginner: Keep pets from eating the plant, and only cook with your own lavender that has not been sprayed. If a pet eats a lot, call your vet.
seasoned: Keep pets from grazing on lavender, and use only your own unsprayed plants, never florist or nursery stock, for any culinary use. If a pet eats a large amount, contact your veterinarian.

beginner: In the northern part of the country, grow English lavender. It is the toughest kind and comes back year after year in zones 5, 6, and 7, where it lives in the ground, flowers in early summer, and gets trimmed back after it blooms. In the very coldest zones (3 and 4), winters are too harsh for it to survive outside, so grow it as a one-season plant or, better, in a pot you bring somewhere sheltered for winter. seasoned: Across the northern tier, English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) is the species to grow: it is reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9 and survives zone 4 with sharp drainage and winter protection. In zones 3 and 4, winters are too cold for it to overwinter reliably in the ground, so it is grown as an annual or, better, in a container that you move to a protected spot for winter. The tender Spanish and French lavenders are not cold-hardy anywhere in this region and are container plants brought in for winter. Wherever you grow it, the real risk is wet feet in winter, not cold alone: lavender rots in soggy, frozen-then-thawing soil, so plant it high and lean with excellent drainage.

English lavender is both the hardiest type and the one used in cooking, while the showy Spanish and French types are tender and ornamental.
